title_options: Why Cars Are Built To Crumple 🚗
facts: Newton's second law: average force = change in momentum / stopping time. Same car, same speed, so the same change in momentum; a longer stop means a smaller average force on the people inside.

Crumple zone: Bela Barenyi, Daimler-Benz patent DBP 854 157, filed 23 Jan 1951, granted 28 Aug 1952; first series-production car with crumple zones: Mercedes-Benz W 111, 1959 (German Patent and Trade Mark Office; Mercedes-Benz history).
Rigid passenger cell between soft front and rear zones (Barenyi's design).
description: A car that folds up in a crash keeps you safer than one that doesn't. Here's the physics: the same stop, spread over more time, needs less force. #shorts #physics #science #cars
sources: Newton's second law (impulse); Bela Barenyi crumple-zone patent DBP 854 157 (filed 1951, granted 1952), German Patent and Trade Mark Office; Mercedes-Benz W 111 (1959), Mercedes-Benz history.

scenes.narration: A car that folds up in a crash keeps you safer than one that doesn't.
Both of these cars hit the wall at the same speed, and both of them stop.
The stiff car stops almost instantly, so the people inside get hit with a huge force.
The folding front makes the stop last longer, so the force on the people inside drops.
That's Newton's second law: the same change in speed, spread over more time, needs less force.
The idea was patented in 1952, and Mercedes-Benz first built it into a production car in 1959.
So why is the middle of the car built to be as strong as possible?
